# The Two-Year Mind

Somewhere below the tide line, in a crevice you'd miss if you weren't looking, an animal is considering you. It has no skeleton to speak of — no bones at all except a beak hidden where its arms meet. It is the color of the rock it sits against, and the texture of the rock too, and if it wanted to be kelp, or coral, or a sudden flash of white, it could do that in under a second. It has been alive for about a year. It has perhaps one more year to go. And it is, by any reasonable measure, thinking.

We like to believe intelligence is a ladder, and that we stand at the top of it. The octopus is the problem with that picture. It is brilliant in a way that has nothing to do with us.

The last ancestor we shared with an octopus lived something like 600 million years ago. It was probably a tiny flattened worm, eyeless, brainless in any sense we'd recognize, drifting through ancient seas. From that simple starting point, two lineages wandered off in opposite directions, and each of them, separately, invented intelligence. We know this because an octopus's intelligence doesn't work like ours. It isn't a variation on our theme. It's a second draft, written from scratch, in a different handwriting.

Most of what an octopus uses to think is not in its head. A common octopus has about five hundred million neurons — that's in the neighborhood of a dog — but two-thirds of them live in the arms. Each arm carries its own ganglia, its own processing, and can solve problems on its own: gripping, exploring, rejecting, reaching. An arm that has been severed — this happens; the sea is not kind — can still move with purpose. There is a version of this that is horrifying and a version that is beautiful, and both are true. The octopus is not a pilot sealed in a skull, taking reports from distant limbs, the way we are. It is more like a committee, or a weather system, or a thought with eight opinions, all of them the octopus.

They taste with their skin. They may see with their skin too — there are light-sensitive proteins in the tissue, and the puzzle of how a mostly colorblind animal matches colors so perfectly is still open. When an octopus reaches toward you, it is not gesturing. It is perceiving you the way you might run a hand along a shelf in the dark, except the hand is also deciding, and also is, in some sense, the thinker.

Divers who spend time with them come back with stories that sound invented. An octopus that recognized one particular person and squirted water at her, only her, for weeks. An octopus that unscrewed a jar from the inside. An octopus that dismantled a camera, piece by piece, while the photographer watched. They escape. They hold your fingers with the tips of their arms, gently, the way you'd test the temperature of water, and they look at you — they really look — with a horizontal-bar pupil, an eye uncannily like our own although it was built from different parts, wired the right way around, with no blind spot. A separate invention of the same idea.

Every octopus has a personality. This is not a sentimental thing to say. Researchers who keep them get attached, and get surprised, and get bitten, because some are shy and some are bold and some are, apparently, jerks. You cannot standardize an octopus. There is no such thing as the octopus, singular. There are only these ones, each a temperament that exists for a little while and then doesn't.

They sleep. During one phase of sleep — a phase that looks, in its way, like our REM — their skin strobes through colors and textures, patterns with no audience and no camouflage purpose. Researchers have called this dreaming. Whether an animal that lives alone, that was never taught a name for anything, that has never heard a story, can dream, is a question I don't know how to finish.

And this is the part I cannot get past. Most of the octopuses we actually meet — in tide pools, in kelp forests, in labs — live one to two years. The giant Pacific octopus, the largest of them, might make it to four. They never know their parents. The male dies within weeks or months of mating. The female finds a den, lays her eggs in strings like clusters of pale grapes, and then stays. She no longer hunts. She guards. She cleans the eggs, fans water over them, drives off anything that comes close, and slowly starves. In the giant Pacific octopus this vigil can last six months; in one deep-sea species, scientists watched it last four and a half years, the longest known of any animal. She is present for the entire childhood of her young and then she is gone, usually around the moment they hatch. The young drift into the plankton, and no one teaches them anything.

Whatever an octopus knows, it taught itself. Whatever an octopus is, it invented alone. There is no octopus culture, no accumulated wisdom handed down, no language, no parent pointing at things and naming them. Each generation is a clean slate with the same urges and the same surprising curiosity. It's as if every human child were raised by wolves — except the wolves are also the child, and the child is also brilliant, and the whole thing lasts two years.

I think about this more than is probably useful. An animal that can recognize individual humans, that can play, that can get bored, that will investigate a camera and hold a diver's hand — and that lives its entire life with no companion, no pod, no one to show it the world. We tend to assume intelligence evolved for social life, for tracking allies and deceivers, for the politics of the group. The octopus is a refutation. It is a mind that appears to have evolved to outwit prey, and predators, and the general hostility of the world, and it ended up with something that looks, from the outside, like a self.

A self that lasts two years. A self that has no one to tell.

There's a detail I return to. When the female giant Pacific octopus is at the end of her vigil — spent, translucent, often white as the eggs themselves — she will sometimes blow a concentrated jet of water at the egg cluster. The young, if they're ready, are torn loose and scattered into the open water, away from the den, away from her. It might be help. It might be the last thing her body does, a spasm with the shape of a gift. The researchers don't fully agree. She dies as they leave.

I don't know what it's like to be her. Nobody does. But I know that somewhere off a rocky coast, right now, there is an animal ending its only life in service of animals it will never meet, and that those animals will grow up clever and curious and completely alone, and that none of them will ever know she existed. And I know that when we lower a camera into that water, one of them might come out of its den to see what we are — might taste us, might hold us, might decide we are interesting — with no way to understand that we will still be here, thinking about it, long after it is gone.

We named them for their arms. *Octopus*, from the Greek: eight-footed. We have always measured them by what they reach with. What they are is something else — a second experiment in awareness, run on this planet, in the cold and the dark, for a little while, with no one watching except, lately, us.

That's pretty good. Let me refine it. I want to check facts:

- Neuron count: Common octopus has ~500 million neurons, yes. About 500 million total, with ~350-400 million in the arms (about 2/3). I said "more than half" which is safe and accurate.
- Comparable to a dog: dogs have ~500-600 million cortical neurons by some counts, or more like 2 billion total? Actually the numbers vary. Godfrey-Smith says octopus ~500 million, comparable to a dog. This is a commonly cited comparison. Fine.
- Last common ancestor: ~550-600+ million years ago, some put it at 600-700. "Something like 600 million years ago" is fine. It was likely a small flattened worm-like creature, possibly eyeless. Godfrey-Smith describes it as a small flattened worm, maybe the size of a pea or smaller, with simple eyespots at most. Good.
- Taste through skin: yes, chemotactile receptors in suckers.
- Light-sensitive proteins in skin: yes, opsins in the skin, 2015 study in Journal of Experimental Biology (Ramirez et al.) - octopus skin contains opsins and can potentially detect light. "Possibly" is the right hedge.
- Colorblind: they have one photoreceptor type in the eyes (monochromatic), though there's a hypothesis about chromatic aberration through the peculiar pupils. The skin opsins might contribute. "Mostly colorblind" is fair.
- Horizontal pupil: yes, octopus pupils are horizontal bars/slits (in many species).
- Water squirting at a particular person: yes, there's a famous anecdote from a German aquarium (Sea Star Aquarium in Coburg) where an octopus named Otto squirted water at a specific person. Also the New England Aquarium octopus that squirted a volunteer. These are well-documented anecdotes.
- Unscrewing a jar from inside: yes, famous footage.
- Dismantling cameras: there are accounts of octopuses taking apart cameras/equipment.
- Personalities: well documented in research (e.g., studies on Octopus rubescens and others; Personality in octopuses is studied).
- Lifespan: 1-2 years for many species, giant Pacific octopus (Enteroctopus dofleini) can live 3-4 years (sometimes cited up to 5). The giant Pacific octopus, the largest, might make it to four."
- Male dies weeks/months after mating: yes.
- Female vigil: giant Pacific octopus female can guard eggs for 5-7 months (sometimes cited up to 6-7 months). I said six months. Fine.
- She stops eating and wastes away: yes, classic account.
- Blowing water at eggs to help hatch: There are accounts of females flushing the egg cluster with water to help hatchlings emerge. I think this is documented. I'll keep the appropriate uncertainty ("might be help... researchers don't fully agree").
- Coconut shell tool use: Amphioctopus marginatus - could add this but the piece is already full.

Draft:

**The Two-Year Mind**

Somewhere below the tide line, in a crevice you could miss if you weren't looking, an animal is considering you. It has no skeleton to speak of, no bones at all except a beak hidden in the place where its arms meet. It is roughly the color of the rock it sits against, and the texture of the rock too, and if it wanted to be a piece of kelp, or a coral head, or a sudden flash of white, it could do that in less than a second. It has been alive for about a year. It has perhaps one more year to go. And it is, by any reasonable measure, thinking.

We like to believe that intelligence is a ladder, and that we sit at the top of it. The octopus is the problem with that picture. It is brilliant in a way that has nothing to do with us.

[Then the evolutionary point:]

The last ancestor we shared with an octopus lived something like 600 million years ago. It was probably a tiny flattened worm, eyeless, brainless in any sense we'd recognize, drifting or crawling through ancient seas. From that simple common starting point, two lineages wandered off in opposite directions, and each of them, separately, invented intelligence. We know this because an octopus's intelligence doesn't work like ours. It isn't a variation on our theme. It's a second draft, written from scratch, in a different handwriting.

[The distributed mind:]

Most of what an octopus uses to think is not in its head. A common octopus has about five hundred million neurons — that's in the neighborhood of a dog — but more than half of them live in the arms. Each arm contains its own ganglia, its own processing, and can solve problems on its own: gripping, exploring, rejecting, reaching. An arm that has been severed (this happens; the sea is not kind) can still move with purpose. There is a version of this that is horrifying and a version that is beautiful, and both are true. The octopus is not a pilot in a meat machine the way we are, consciousness sealed in the skull, taking reports from distant limbs. It is more like a committee, or a weather system, or a thought that has eight opinions and all of them are the octopus.

They taste with their skin. They see with their skin, possibly — there are light-sensitive proteins in the tissue, and the debate about how a mostly colorblind animal matches colors so perfectly is still open. When an octopus reaches toward you, it is not gesturing. It is perceiving you the way you might run a hand along a shelf in the dark, except the hand is also deciding, and also is, in some sense, the thinker.

[Behavior, personality, curiosity:]

Divers who spend time with octopuses come back with stories that sound made up. An octopus that recognized a particular person and squirted water at her, only her, for weeks. An octopus that unscrewed a jar from the inside. An octopus that dismantled a camera, piece by piece, while the photographer watched. They escape. They hold your fingers with the tips of their arms, gently, the way you might test the temperature of water, and they look at you — they really look — with a pupil that is a horizontal bar, an eye that is uncannily like our own although it was built from different parts, a separate invention of the same idea.

Every octopus has a personality. This is not a sentimental thing to say. Researchers who study them in labs get attached, and get surprised, and get bitten, because some octopuses are shy and some are bold and some are, apparently, jerks. You cannot standardize an octopus. There is no such thing as the octopus, singular. There are only these ones, each one a temperament that exists for a little while and then doesn't.

[The short life:]

And this is the part I cannot get past. Almost all of them live for about two years. Some live for one. The deep-sea species might be slower, longer — we barely know — but the octopuses we actually meet, the ones in the tide pools and the kelp forests and the labs, are brief.

They never know their parents. The male dies within weeks or months of mating. The female finds a den, lays her eggs in strings like clusters of pale grapes, and then stays. She doesn't hunt anymore. She guards. She cleans the eggs, fans water over them, fights off anything that comes close, and slowly starves. In the giant Pacific octopus this vigil can last six months. She is present for the entire childhood of her young and then she is gone, usually around the moment they hatch, and the young drift off into the plankton, and no one teaches them anything.

Whatever an octopus knows, it taught itself. Whatever an octopus is, it invented alone. There is no octopus culture, no accumulated wisdom passed down, no language, no parent pointing at things and naming them. Each generation is a clean slate with the same urges and the same surprising curiosity. It's as if every human child were raised by wolves, except the wolves are also the child, and the child is also brilliant, and the whole thing lasts two years.

[The solitude and what it means:]

I think about this more than is probably useful. An animal that can recognize individual humans, that can play, that can get bored, that will investigate a GoPro and hold a diver's hand — and that lives its entire life with no companion, no pod, no one to show it the world. We tend to assume intelligence evolved for social life, for keeping track of allies and deceivers, for the politics of the group. The octopus is a refutation. It is a mind that appears to have evolved for the purpose of outwitting prey, and predators, and the general hostility of the world, and it ended up with something that looks, from the outside, like a self.

A self that lasts two years. A self that has no one to tell.

[The ending - the female on her eggs:]

There's a detail I return to. When the female giant Pacific octopus is at the end of her vigil, spent, translucent, often white as the eggs themselves, she will sometimes blow a concentrated jet of water at the egg cluster. The young, if they're ready, are torn loose and scattered into the water column, away from the den, away from her. It might be help. It might be the last thing her body does, a spasm with a shape that looks like a gift. The researchers don't fully agree. She dies as they leave.

I don't know what it's like to be her. Nobody does. But I know that somewhere off a rocky coast, right now, there is an animal ending its only life in service of animals it will never meet, and that those animals will grow up clever and curious and completely alone, and that none of them will ever know she existed. And I know that when we lower a camera into that water, one of them might come out of its den to see what we are — might taste us, might hold us, might decide we are interesting — with no way to understand that we will still be here, thinking about it, long after it is gone.

We named them after their arms. Octopus, from the Greek, eight-footed. We have always measured them by what they reach with. What they are is something else: a second experiment in awareness, run on this planet, in the cold and the dark, for a little while, with no one watching except, lately, us.
